newsitem.title: PERU: Peru maps out strategy ahead of fresh rebel talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru maps out strategy ahead of fresh rebel talks.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori and his Cabinet on Thursday mapped out Peru's strategy for the next round of face-to-face talks, expected by Saturday, with Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home.

Following his arrival in Lima late on Wednesday from London, Fujimori met with his ministers at Government Palace to be debriefed on Tuesday's meeting, the first between the two sides since Dec. 28 last year.

At that meeting Peru's negotiator, Domingo Palermo, and the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, agreed to press on with negotiations to find a solution to the 58-day siege.

A top government source close to the negotiations told Reuters he expected the two men to meet again on Friday or Saturday. The talks will take place across the street from the diplomatic compound in the same Red Cross safe house specially rented for Tuesday's talks.

After weeks of deadlock, the resumption of dialogue has marked a breakthrough in the crisis. But with the rebels refusing to give up their demand for the release of hundreds of comrades -- a demand the government flatly rejects -- a peaceful solution is not expected any time soon.
Holed-up in the envoy's mansion for over eight weeks, the hostages are showing deepening signs of physical and mental strain.
The Red Cross, which is both mediating in the crisis and providing humanitarian aid to the hostages, on Thursday stepped up its medical activities inside the compound.

The organisation laid cables to carry electricity into the fortified embassy residence for the first time since the early days of the siege. Red Cross officials said three specialist doctors would use the electricity for equipment they took into the residence. The officials did not elaborate.
The Red Cross, coordinating its work from a house near the compound, also stocked up on medical supplies, including wheelchairs.

The last two releases from the compound have been on medical grounds and relatives claim several remaining captives are seriously ill. Aid workers and police say that most hostages are being treated for ailments such as hypertension, digestive problems or depression.
Both sides have sought to avoid harming the hostages but Fujimori has warned he will only rule out using force to end the siege while all the hostages remain unharmed.
Amid fears the crisis could drag on for weeks, Peru's top Roman Catholic priest urged the MRTA to end the "agony" of the siege immediately.
Cardinal Augusto Vargas Alzamora on Wednesday exhorted the MRTA "to say 'we renounce holding them any longer.'"
"Peru would applaud their example. But if they prolong this agony any longer, Peru will repudiate them." he told reporters.
Despite local disappointment at the apparent lack of concrete progress at Tuesday's talks, foreign governments reacted with cautious optimism to the dialogue.

The U.S. State Department, viewing it as a "positive step" toward a peaceful solution, said: "The fact that they, after so many weeks, have arrived at the point where they can talk to each other directly in a rational way is a strong indicator that a peaceful solution is possible."
Japan's Foreign Ministry said it hoped the talks "will pave the way for the start of full negotiations so that the incident can be solved peacefully and the hostages freed early."

Japan has urged Fujimori to seek a peaceful outcome, but there is also strong endorsement from U.S. President Bill Clinton among others for his refusal to consider the MRTA's main demand for the release of comrades.

"The United States does not believe that terrorists should succeed and we do not believe that concessions should be made to them," U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns commented on Wednesday.
Fujimori's brother and a brother-in-law are among the 72 remaining hostages, who also include two government ministers, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia and about two dozen Japanese businessmen.
